THE BUILD

Where are the datacentres, and what is the power and water around them doing?

Every datacentre OpenStreetMap has mapped in the United States, plus the ones it has mapped as under construction or proposed, joined to the drought in their county, the nearest river gauge /watts reads, and the grid they sit on.

This is a map of buildings, not of electricity. 1,877 datacentres have been mapped in the United States by volunteers; 1,350 of them — 72% — stand in a county the US Drought Monitor placed in a drought category this week, and 371 sit on one of the three grids that publish a demand number without an account. What any of these buildings actually draws is not published by anyone.

  • 1,877 mapped sites 1,877 carry surveyed coordinates
  • 95 under construction a hole in the ground and a crane, in OpenStreetMap
  • 13 announced located to the evidence, never more precisely
  • 1,350 in a county in drought 534 of them in D2 or worse
  • 371 with a live grid number 1,506 sit on a grid with no keyless feed

What this map cannot show you

Nothing here measures a datacentre’s power or water draw. No public feed publishes either, for any site, at any cadence. What is measured is where the buildings are and what the substrate around them is doing — which is a smaller claim, and a true one.

A state with no pins is a state nobody has mapped. It is not a state with no datacentres. OpenStreetMap coverage is volunteer-maintained and uneven. Virginia has 407 pins and Wyoming has 23; some of that is the build-out and some of it is who maps.

Capacity is tagged on 43 of 1,877 sites, totalling 2,374.6 MW of tagged IT power. Any sum over this dataset is a sum over two per cent of it, which is why no total megawatt figure is printed anywhere on this page.

“Operating” means the building exists. It is not a claim that there are servers in it, that they are switched on, or that they are training anything. A decommissioned datacentre keeps its tag until somebody visits. A map is extremely persuasive, and that is exactly why it has to say all of this before it draws anything.

What moves between collects

3 of 11 balancing authorities publish a number without an account. These are the only figures on this page that can differ from the ones you saw last time.

  • this collect 2026-09-26 16:22:02 UTC the run that wrote every pin above
  • ERCOT 63.65% of committed capacity ERCOT headroom used · observed 2026-09-26 16:20:00 UTC AWAITING BASELINE
  • CAISO 22,590MW CAISO overnight floor · observed 2026-09-26 16:21:59 UTC AWAITING BASELINE
  • NYISO 12,196MW NYISO overnight floor · observed 2026-09-26 08:15:00 UTC AWAITING BASELINE
  • drought map 2026-09-22 weekly, published Thursdays LIVE
  • streamflow day 2026-09-25 day of year, against each gauge's own long-run median LIVE

There is no new-sites line here, and that is deliberate. Every one of the 1,877 sites in this file carries the same first_seen_at — 2026-09-26 16:22:02 UTC — which is this run's own timestamp. The field is stamped at collect time rather than carried forward, so it cannot separate a site found today from one found last week. A diff built on it would announce 1,877 new sites on every single run, which is a fabricated event dressed as a measurement. The pins move when OpenStreetMap moves, which is on volunteer time, not on a cron.

The map 1,877

Three controls sit on top of this picture and none of them needs JavaScript: shape, colour, and one of 49 jurisdictions. They dim the map rather than cutting it, the count beside every chip is the count you get if you press it, and the figure in the readout is already in this HTML for all 16 combinations — so it cannot lag the control and cannot be wrong in a screenshot.

3 controls · 800 states of this page · every one already in this HTML

These controls dim. They never remove. 1,877 pins and 49 table rows stay in the page at every setting, because a filter that deletes rows is a filter that can hide a source that went dark. Focusing a jurisdiction dims every pin that is not recorded in it, including any pin with no state recorded at all — unknown is not the same as elsewhere. 0 of 1,877 sites are in that position in this build.

Shape is status

  • operating 1,769
  • under construction 95
  • announced 13

Distinguishable in greyscale and in a screenshot. These three are the map's small-scale form of the same three statuses the rest of this page marks with the site's own icons: a datacentre pin is under five pixels across at national scale, which is below the size a drawn footprint survives at. Status is read from the OpenStreetMap tag that set it, and every pin carries that tag in the JSON.

Colour is the drought in that county

  • none 527
  • D0 abnormally dry 179
  • D1 moderate 637
  • D2 severe 165
  • D3 extreme 298
  • D4 exceptional 71

US Drought Monitor, week of 2026-09-22. Every count here is also printed in words, because a reader who cannot separate two of these hues still gets the number. 1,350 of 1,877 pins sit in a county carrying a category.

Size is capacity, where it is published

  • fixed dot 1,834 — known site, capacity unpublished
  • ringed and scaled 43 — an IT-power tag exists
  • river gauge 9 — one of the 9 Watts reads

A pin is 2.4 units across unless OpenStreetMap carries an IT-power tag for it, in which case its radius is 3 + 0.55 × √MW, capped at 10, and it is drawn half-transparent with a ring. No pin is ever sized by a guess: a site with no capacity tag gets the fixed dot.

The water

Drought is the resource this map can actually carry, because the US Drought Monitor publishes it by county and every pin has a county. It is the colour of every dot above. 1,350 of 1,877 pins stand in a county carrying a category on the map dated 2026-09-22, and 534 of those are in D2 or worse.

  • none 527 28.1%
  • D0 abnormally dry 179 9.5%
  • D1 moderate 637 33.9%
  • D2 severe 165 8.8%
  • D3 extreme 298 15.9%
  • D4 exceptional 71 3.8%

Drought figures are the share of a county’s AREA in a category. A county 20% in D3 does not say which 20%, and the Drought Monitor is a weekly expert judgement, not an instrument reading.

The power

Every pin is assigned to the balancing authority that runs its state's grid, with named county exceptions where that is wrong. Three of those authorities publish a real-time number without an account, and they cover 371 of 1,877 pins. The single largest block on this map — 681 pins on PJM — is not one of them.

A blank cell reads as an oversight. A named wall reads as a boundary of the instrument, which is what it is. Every grid below with no number says why in its own words, and those words are the same ones Watts prints for the same grid.

How this was built, and what is wrong with it

Status, in words

  • operating — a building that exists. Not a claim that servers are in it and running.
  • under construction — tagged in OpenStreetMap as under construction — a hole in the ground and a crane.
  • announced — somebody said it is being built. Location is as precise as the evidence, and never more.

Confidence, in words

Confidence is a statement about the record, not about the building.

  • high — named, with an operator, and carrying a capacity tag.
  • medium — named, with an operator.
  • low — a mapped polygon with no name or no operator, or a single unconfirmed announcement.

The sources

Every source, its state on this build, and where its bytes came from — network, cache, stale cache or local file. A stale cache is not a live read and is never printed as one. The count is what the source returned, before the county filter: OpenStreetMap answered with 1,958 elements over three bounding boxes that necessarily include Canada, Mexico and the Caribbean, and 81 of them were in no US county and were dropped rather than placed.
SourceSites StateError
OpenStreetMap datacentre tags, via Overpassoperating and under-construction sites, with surveyed coordinates 1,958 LIVEvia cache no error
Announcements extracted from the DOOMCON newsroomannounced sites, state-level, traceable to a scored news item id 0 LIVEvia local no error
Federal Register documents naming a datacentre projectannounced sites named in a federal notice, state-level 0 LIVEvia network no error
SEC filings saying "data centers", joined to operatorsoperator-level corroboration; no pins, no coordinates 0 LIVEvia network no error
Census TIGERweb county boundaries — LIVEvia cache no error
USGS site service — coordinates for the nine /watts gauges 9 LIVEvia cache no error
US Drought Monitor, county statistics — LIVE no error

Every limitation, in full

  1. OpenStreetMap coverage is uneven and volunteer-maintained. A datacentre missing from this map means nobody mapped it, not that it does not exist.
  2. Capacity tags are rare: 43 of 1877 sites carry one.
  3. Nothing here measures a datacentre’s power or water draw. No feed publishes that for any site at any cadence. What is measured is the condition of the substrate around it.
  4. Announced sites are announcements. Their location is the state that was named, never a surveyed address, and every one carries the document or news item it came from.
  5. Drought figures are the share of a county’s AREA in a category. A county 20% in D3 does not say which 20%, and the Drought Monitor is a weekly expert judgement, not an instrument reading.
  6. The nearest river gauge is one of the nine /watts reads. Each pin carries the distance to it, because a gauge 300 km away describes a different watershed.
  7. A balancing authority is not a state. ERCOT, NYISO and CAISO are assigned by state with named county exceptions; everything else carries the reason there is no keyless feed.
  8. Three states stay apart everywhere: a live reading, a reading awaiting its baseline, and a dark source. None of them is imputed into another.

Two of the sources share one host, and the whole existing half of this map depends on a single volunteer-run Overpass instance. Three mirrors and a seven-day disk cache are the only redundancy there is. Sites geocode against Census county polygons simplified to about 550 metres, so a site on a county line can land in the neighbouring county; 66 pins carry that flag.

What was tried and dropped

The Federal Register names no datacentre projects: of 437 documents whose full text carries the phrase over eighteen months, four have it in the title and not one of them is a project — a flight-data web portal, a paediatric emergency data repository, a permitting executive order and a listening session. SEC full-text search returns the filer's registered head office rather than the site, so it adds no pins and is used only to corroborate an operator. Full OpenStreetMap geometry would give a footprint area at roughly ten times the payload and a materially higher chance of the query timing out on a server that was already refusing requests; that trade was made in favour of the query completing, which is why there is no area field anywhere on this page.

Streamflow day 2026-09-25, LIVE. This does not feed the DOOMCON index and has no route into it: collector/engine.mjs does not read this file, and none of these sources sits in the frozen reference distribution the composite is scored against.

Same subject, different instrument

Watts — the infrastructure index

This page asks where the buildings are. Watts asks how the substrate is holding up: grid overnight floors in three control regions, streamflow at the nine gauges above, drought across ten states, and the SEC and Federal Register paper trail, scored on to a five-stop scale. Every grid number and every gauge reading on this page is the same reading Watts prints, read from the same run.

AI Early Warning System

Detected early, never predicted. We just count.

DOOMCON measures how much is happening, not how bad it is. Levels describe observable activity tempo against this index’s own record. They are not a probability of harm.

The desk

  • IndexThe composite, the five pillars, the live signal feed.
  • The RaceFrontier labs ranked on live prediction-market odds.
  • NewsroomEvery story, scored on how many independent sources carried it.
  • WattsThe substrate index: grid load, drought and buildout under the models.
  • MapWhere the compute physically sits, against the water it needs.
  • CamerasAutomated licence-plate readers, as volunteers have mapped them into OpenStreetMap.
  • LeadersWhat the people running AI said this week, as their publishers printed it.
  • DigestThe day in one page, assembled from the scored corpus.
  • BlissThe same machinery, pointed the other way.
  • MethodologyEvery formula and constant. Recompute the number yourself.
  • HistorySixty years of the same argument, dated and attributed.
  • ArchiveEvery scored observation, each with a hash-chained receipt.

Data

  • JSON APILevel, score, pillars, per-source health.
  • History JSONEvery scored observation as one file.
  • HealthPer-source success, honestly reported.
  • EmbedOne iframe. No script, no key, no tracking.
  • RSSAn entry per index move.
  • ALPR JSONMapped ALPR cameras by state and by county — including the 948 counties nobody has mapped.
  • ALPR pointsPacked latitude, longitude and bearing, one entry per mapped camera. OpenStreetMap data, ODbL.

Collection runs on a published */15 cron; scheduled runs are queued and are routinely late, which is why the rail above says overdue rather than counting down into fiction. Every value on this site is computed from public data by published code, and each observation is written to a hash-chained receipt carrying its full inputs — so anyone can recompute the number and get the same answer.
